steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the Implementations section of an encyclopedia article on the AX.25 amateur packet radio protocol, covering hardware TNCs, software implementations on PCs, and the KISS framing used between host and TNC.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Terminal node controllers (TNCs)
- AX.25 on personal computers (Linux, BPQ over Ethernet)
- Dire Wolf software TNC
## KISS-mode framing
- What KISS is and why it is used
- Limitations and alternatives

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- TNCs
  - traditional way amateur radio operators connect to AX.25 networks
  - microprocessor + protocol implemented in firmware
  - only need a dumb terminal and a transceiver
- PCs
  - Linux kernel long had native AX.25 support
  - computer -> transceiver via audio interface or simple modem
  - BPQ over Ethernet framing (also native in Linux): interconnect computers, bridge/route to remote TNCs and transceivers
  - lets transceivers sit under/in the antenna mast: 'low loss', shorter RF wiring; cheap fiber (RFI both ways/EMP/lightning resistant) or copper Ethernet replaces expensive long thick coax and amplifiers
  - stacks of TNC+transceiver pairs on any computer network; all radio links accessible simultaneously (transparently bridged); talk to each other internally over AX.25; or filtered routing to pick specific TNCs/frequencies
- Dire Wolf
  - free open-source replacement for 1980s-style TNC
  - DSP software modems; full AX25 v2.2 + FX.25 forward error correction
  - digital repeater, GPS tracker, APRS Internet Gateway (IGate), no extra software
## KISS-mode framing
- (see main article: KISS (TNC))
- TNC implementing KISS framing = low-cost alternative to expensive, uncommon HDLC controller cards
- not part of AX.25, not sent over the air; just encapsulates frames over serial link to TNC
- derived from SLIP; same assumptions, e.g. only two "endpoints"
  - SLIP: two SLIP-connected hosts; KISS: host computer + TNC over serial
  - awkward to address multiple TNCs without multiple serial channels
- alternatives addressing this: 6PACK

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Traditionally amateur radio operators connected to AX.25 networks by using a terminal node controller. A terminal node controller has a microprocessor in it and the protocol is implemented in firmware. With these devices you can access network resources using just a dumb terminal and a transceiver.

AX.25 has also been implemented on personal computers. For example the Linux kernel has had native support for AX.25 for a long time. The computer is connected to a transceiver through its audio interface or through a simple modem. Computers can also be connected to other computers, or bridged or routed to TNCs and transceivers somewhere else, using BPQ over Ethernet framing. This is also supported natively by the Linux kernel, and it makes more modern setups possible where the actual transceivers are placed directly under or in the antenna mast. That gives 'low loss' and shorter RF wiring, and the expensive, long and thick coax cables and amplifiers are replaced with cheap fiber (which is RFI (both ways)/EMP/lightning resistant) or copper Ethernet wiring. With BPQ Ethernet framing you can connect whole stacks of TNC+transceiver pairs to any existing computer network, and then all the computers can access all the radio links at the same time (transparently bridged), communicate with each other internally over AX.25, or use filtered routing to select specific TNCs/radio frequencies.

Dire Wolf is a free open-source replacement for the 1980s-style TNC. It has DSP software modems and a complete implementation of AX25 v2.2 plus FX.25 forward error correction. Without any other software it can work as a digital repeater, a GPS tracker, and an APRS Internet Gateway (IGate).

## KISS-mode framing

- (see main article: KISS (TNC))
- TNC with KISS framing = low-cost alternative to expensive, uncommon HDLC controller cards
- not part of AX.25, not sent over the air; just encapsulates frames over serial link to TNC
- derived from SLIP; same assumptions, e.g. only two "endpoints"
  - SLIP: two SLIP-connected hosts; KISS: host computer + TNC over serial
  - awkward to address multiple TNCs without multiple serial channels
- alternatives: 6PACK

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Traditionally amateur radio operators connected to AX.25 networks by using a terminal node controller. A terminal node controller has a microprocessor in it and the protocol is implemented in firmware. With these devices you can access network resources using just a dumb terminal and a transceiver.

AX.25 has also been implemented on personal computers. For example the Linux kernel has had native support for AX.25 for a long time. The computer is connected to a transceiver through its audio interface or through a simple modem. Computers can also be connected to other computers, or bridged or routed to TNCs and transceivers somewhere else, using BPQ over Ethernet framing. This is also supported natively by the Linux kernel, and it makes more modern setups possible where the actual transceivers are placed directly under or in the antenna mast. That gives 'low loss' and shorter RF wiring, and the expensive, long and thick coax cables and amplifiers are replaced with cheap fiber (which is RFI (both ways)/EMP/lightning resistant) or copper Ethernet wiring. With BPQ Ethernet framing you can connect whole stacks of TNC+transceiver pairs to any existing computer network, and then all the computers can access all the radio links at the same time (transparently bridged), communicate with each other internally over AX.25, or use filtered routing to select specific TNCs/radio frequencies.

Dire Wolf is a free open-source replacement for the 1980s-style TNC. It has DSP software modems and a complete implementation of AX25 v2.2 plus FX.25 forward error correction. Without any other software it can work as a digital repeater, a GPS tracker, and an APRS Internet Gateway (IGate).

## KISS-mode framing

See full article at KISS (TNC)

AX.25 is often used together with a TNC that implements KISS framing. This is a low-cost alternative to using HDLC controller cards, which are expensive and not common.

KISS framing is not part of the AX.25 protocol and it is not sent over the air. All it does is encapsulate the protocol frames so they can get across a serial link to the TNC. KISS framing comes from Serial Line Internet Protocol (SLIP) and it makes a lot of the same assumptions, for example that only two "endpoints" are involved in the conversation. In SLIP these were the two hosts connected by SLIP, and in KISS it is assumed that the KISS framing link goes over serial and only the host computer and the TNC are involved. One result of this is that it is awkward to address multiple TNCs unless you have multiple (serial) data channels.

There are alternatives to KISS that address these limitations, for example 6PACK.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Traditionally, amateur radio operators have connected to AX.25 networks using a terminal node controller, which contains a microprocessor and an implementation of the protocol in firmware. These devices allow network resources to be accessed with only a dumb terminal and a transceiver.

AX.25 has also been implemented on personal computers. For example, the Linux kernel has long included native support for AX.25.[1] The computer connects to a transceiver via its audio interface or via a simple modem. Computers can also interconnect with other computers, or be bridged or routed to TNCs and transceivers located elsewhere, using BPQ over Ethernet framing. This is also natively supported by the Linux kernel and makes more modern setups possible, with the actual transceivers placed directly under or in the antenna mast, giving 'low loss', shorter RF wiring and replacing expensive, long and thick coax cables and amplifiers with cheap fiber (RFI (both ways)/EMP/lightning resistant) or copper Ethernet wiring. BPQ Ethernet framing allows entire stacks of TNC+transceiver pairs to be connected to any existing computer network; the computers can then all access all radio links offered simultaneously (transparently bridged), communicate with each other internally over AX.25, or select specific TNCs/radio frequencies with filtered routing.

Dire Wolf is a free open-source replacement for the 1980s-style TNC. It contains DSP software modems and a complete implementation of AX25 v2.2 plus FX.25 forward error correction. It can function as a digital repeater, GPS tracker, and APRS Internet Gateway (IGate) without any additional software.

## KISS-mode framing

See full article at KISS (TNC)

AX.25 is often used with a TNC that implements the KISS[2] framing, as a low-cost alternative to expensive and uncommon HDLC controller cards.

The KISS framing is not part of the AX.25 protocol itself, and it is not sent over the air. It only serves to encapsulate the protocol frames so that they can pass over a serial link to the TNC. KISS framing is derived from Serial Line Internet Protocol (SLIP) and makes many of the same assumptions, such as there being only two "endpoints" in the conversation. With SLIP these were the two SLIP-connected hosts; with KISS, the framing link is assumed to be over serial with only the host computer and the TNC involved. Among other things, this makes it awkward to address multiple TNCs without having multiple (serial) data channels.

Alternatives to KISS that address these limitations do exist, such as 6PACK.[3,4]

References:
[1] John Ackermann. (2002). Linux AX.25 Configuration. febo.com. http://www.febo.com/packet/linux-ax25/index.html
[2] Mike Chepponis. The KISS TNC: A simple Host-to-TNC communications protocol. http://www.ka9q.net/papers/kiss.html
[3] 6PACK a "real time" PC to TNC protocol. http://private.freepage.de/cgi-bin/feets/freepage_ext/41030x030A/rewrite/alexs/xfr/flexnet/6pack_en/6pack.htm
[4] 6pack Protocol - The Linux Kernel
